title: Could Agentic AI Bring American Manufacturing Back?

As engineering talent becomes harder to find, Agentic AI can help manufacturers boost productivity while keeping human expertise essential
Deposit Photos
Imagine an aviation supplier received the good news it had been waiting years for: the awarding of a massive contract for a next-generation jet. This project is the shot in the arm it needs to get out of the red and into the black. The problem is the manufacturer does not employ enough engineers to take it on. Either it must offshore the work or stretch the delivery timeline.
The Problematic Personnel Bottleneck
Though this story is fictional, the conundrum it depicts is very real. There just aren't enough skilled American engineers to meet demand.
The aerospace sector is feeling this paucity. "'Our Corporate Members tell us there are not enough people studying engineering to fill the jobs of the future,' says Vickie Singer, senior director of Revenue Development and Corporate Membership for AIAA, the world's largest technical society dedicated to the global aerospace profession," reports Aerospace America .
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the same source, the pool of competent engineers has shrunk post-COVID. The talent drain is only expected to intensify as older workers and managers age out of their present roles.
Jeff Immelt has had a closeup view of this decline. As the former chairman and CEO of General Electric, succeeding Jack Welch, he can recall an era in which engineering firms could recruit and retain the very best talent it takes to keep domestic industry humming. Not anymore, he told me in an interview.
A venture partner at New Enterprise Associates (NEA), Immelt recently joined the board of directors of P-1 AI, Inc. , an Agentic AI engineering startup for industrial teams that just announced the initial closing of its $50 million Series A financing round. I spoke to Immelt and P-1 AI's co-founder and CEO Paul Eremenko, who was previously the CTO of Airbus, about how investments in capital, technology and personnel can jumpstart America's engineering base.
Both Immelt and Eremenko pinpointed misguided incentives as contributors to the problem. Eremenko sees a cultural element at work. "As a society, we said software engineering is where it's at. Mechanical, electrical, aerospace and industrial engineering have not been glorified as sexy disciplines. And so kids who are inclined toward STEM chose software versus physical forms of engineering, and as a result we lag in our industrial workforce as a country." In other words, America stopped producing the kinds of people who produce things.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Enter artificial intelligence.
An AI Teammate, Not An AI Replacement
P-1 AI believes it's possible to restore domestic production by marrying human teams with machine smarts in the form of Archie, an Agentic AI engineer for mechanical, electrical, thermal and systems design. Eremenko describes Archie less as a software product and more as a hire. "In general, engineering teams are five to 10 people," he explained. "Our thesis is there should be one Archie per team. We're not suggesting that there should be teams that are entirely Archies, or even a team that's half Archies. Archie is the junior guy on every team."
"The idea of plugging in a technology enhancement tool right alongside an engineer, doing side by side tasks for the purpose of doing it faster, more economically, fits the workflow of how companies think about designing products," Immelt added.
The Goal: Doing More with Less
While P-1 AI is focused on data center engineering, automotive and aerospace and defense, the overall notion of an AI stepping in to provide a layer of intelligence on top of human workers dovetails with my recent Forbes article describing how agents can also assist with warehouse productivity, specifically streamlining the factory quoting process that is so integral to profitability and yet so time-consuming.
Advertisement
Advertisement
There's another element at play here that connects with my other recent coverage, specifically a concept I dubbed the Micro-Enterprise Model with applications to GE of all companies. Back in the twentieth century, when this corporate leviathan reigned supreme, size was a proxy for power. The more people you employed, the more capable your organization became at executing complex operations.
Agentic AI changes that calculus, as Archie demonstrates. In the 2020s, aerospace firms like the hypothetical version above needn't strain under a lack of personnel. Instead, tomorrow's engineering outfits can boost human acumen with AI teammates. "By fitting naturally into how engineers collaborate, P-1 AI can shorten cycle times, improve competitiveness and deliver measurable results in mission-critical environments," Immelt said in a statement announcing the round.
Manufacturing Isn't the Only Industry To Benefit
The precedent of multiplying human productivity in this way is already visible. Engineering isn't the only field suffering from a lack of human talent. "The construction industry needs to attract an estimated 349,000 net new workers in 2026 to meet demand for construction services," reports LBM Journal , citing a proprietary model from Associated Builders and Contractors. Already, several solutions exist in the market that echo Archie's teammate-for-the-trades model, including Drawer AI, which supports electrical contractors with items such as "device counting, branch routing, and wire sizing, producing detailed quantity reports and layouts in minutes," according to BuiltWorlds .
Likewise, it is well known that America suffers from a shortage of nurses, a deficit poised to worsen as so many Baby Boomers require increasing healthcare services. Hospitals are rolling out AI scribes to provide a similar human and machine synthesis to fill the gap.
Advertisement
Advertisement
As the American Hospital Association reports, "A recent study published in JAMA found that AI-powered ambient scribes modestly decreased total electronic health record (EHR) time by 13.4 minutes and documentation time by 16.0 minutes across five academic medical centers. The sites included in the study utilized Ambience, Nuance Dragon Ambient eXperience (DAX) Copilot (the predecessor to Microsoft Dragon Copilot) and/or Abridge along with Epic as their EHR system."
Bringing Manufacturing Back Online
Returning to the challenge of onshoring American engineering, Immelt is bullish for the future, thanks to the boon of AI teammates. "Much of the outsourcing over the last few decades was a wage arbitrage play," he explained. Tools like Archie homogenize the wage piece, restoring the business case for building domestically. "If I were a CEO today, I would be confident that I could make whatever I wanted, wherever I wanted to make it, thanks to AI. And if your largest market is the U.S., that is where you will want to make your product."
We can imagine a scenario in which the aviation supplier from our story and other firms needn't turn away or delay work, now aided by an artificial intelligence layer. In that future, teams may still resemble those of today, only each possesses an AI teammate. Eremenko predicts such hybrids could reshore some of America's engineering competitive advantage while expanding "our bandwidth as a species to design the physical world: the megacities, the rocket ships, the space data centers and eventually the starships." The sky is the limit.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

As engineering talent becomes harder to find, Agentic AI can help manufacturers boost productivity while keeping human expertise essential
Deposit Photos
Imagine an aviation supplier received the good news it had been waiting years for: the awarding of a massive contract for a next-generation jet. This project is the shot in the arm it needs to get out of the red and into the black. The problem is the manufacturer does not employ enough engineers to take it on. Either it must offshore the work or stretch the delivery timeline.
The Problematic Personnel Bottleneck
Though this story is fictional, the conundrum it depicts is very real. There just aren't enough skilled American engineers to meet demand.
The aerospace sector is feeling this paucity. "'Our Corporate Members tell us there are not enough people studying engineering to fill the jobs of the future,' says Vickie Singer, senior director of Revenue Development and Corporate Membership for AIAA, the world's largest technical society dedicated to the global aerospace profession," reports Aerospace America .

According to the same source, the pool of competent engineers has shrunk post-COVID. The talent drain is only expected to intensify as older workers and managers age out of their present roles.
Jeff Immelt has had a closeup view of this decline. As the former chairman and CEO of General Electric, succeeding Jack Welch, he can recall an era in which engineering firms could recruit and retain the very best talent it takes to keep domestic industry humming. Not anymore, he told me in an interview.
A venture partner at New Enterprise Associates (NEA), Immelt recently joined the board of directors of P-1 AI, Inc. , an Agentic AI engineering startup for industrial teams that just announced the initial closing of its $50 million Series A financing round. I spoke to Immelt and P-1 AI's co-founder and CEO Paul Eremenko, who was previously the CTO of Airbus, about how investments in capital, technology and personnel can jumpstart America's engineering base.
Both Immelt and Eremenko pinpointed misguided incentives as contributors to the problem. Eremenko sees a cultural element at work. "As a society, we said software engineering is where it's at. Mechanical, electrical, aerospace and industrial engineering have not been glorified as sexy disciplines. And so kids who are inclined toward STEM chose software versus physical forms of engineering, and as a result we lag in our industrial workforce as a country." In other words, America stopped producing the kinds of people who produce things.

Enter artificial intelligence.
An AI Teammate, Not An AI Replacement
P-1 AI believes it's possible to restore domestic production by marrying human teams with machine smarts in the form of Archie, an Agentic AI engineer for mechanical, electrical, thermal and systems design. Eremenko describes Archie less as a software product and more as a hire. "In general, engineering teams are five to 10 people," he explained. "Our thesis is there should be one Archie per team. We're not suggesting that there should be teams that are entirely Archies, or even a team that's half Archies. Archie is the junior guy on every team."
"The idea of plugging in a technology enhancement tool right alongside an engineer, doing side by side tasks for the purpose of doing it faster, more economically, fits the workflow of how companies think about designing products," Immelt added.
The Goal: Doing More with Less
While P-1 AI is focused on data center engineering, automotive and aerospace and defense, the overall notion of an AI stepping in to provide a layer of intelligence on top of human workers dovetails with my recent Forbes article describing how agents can also assist with warehouse productivity, specifically streamlining the factory quoting process that is so integral to profitability and yet so time-consuming.

There's another element at play here that connects with my other recent coverage, specifically a concept I dubbed the Micro-Enterprise Model with applications to GE of all companies. Back in the twentieth century, when this corporate leviathan reigned supreme, size was a proxy for power. The more people you employed, the more capable your organization became at executing complex operations.
Agentic AI changes that calculus, as Archie demonstrates. In the 2020s, aerospace firms like the hypothetical version above needn't strain under a lack of personnel. Instead, tomorrow's engineering outfits can boost human acumen with AI teammates. "By fitting naturally into how engineers collaborate, P-1 AI can shorten cycle times, improve competitiveness and deliver measurable results in mission-critical environments," Immelt said in a statement announcing the round.
Manufacturing Isn't the Only Industry To Benefit
The precedent of multiplying human productivity in this way is already visible. Engineering isn't the only field suffering from a lack of human talent. "The construction industry needs to attract an estimated 349,000 net new workers in 2026 to meet demand for construction services," reports LBM Journal , citing a proprietary model from Associated Builders and Contractors. Already, several solutions exist in the market that echo Archie's teammate-for-the-trades model, including Drawer AI, which supports electrical contractors with items such as "device counting, branch routing, and wire sizing, producing detailed quantity reports and layouts in minutes," according to BuiltWorlds .
Likewise, it is well known that America suffers from a shortage of nurses, a deficit poised to worsen as so many Baby Boomers require increasing healthcare services. Hospitals are rolling out AI scribes to provide a similar human and machine synthesis to fill the gap.
